findings.claim: Item 1 states, for every elliptic curve E over a CM field F, that 'for every m ≥ 0 there is a finite extension F′/F over which Symm^m of the compatible system H¹(E) becomes automorphic', and that 'consequently the Sato–Tate conjecture holds for E'. With 'automorphic' in the paper's own §7.1 sense (attached to a regular algebraic cuspidal π of GL_{m+1}), this is false when E has CM by an imaginary quadratic field K: over any F′ the system Symm^m H¹(E)|G_{F′} is reducible for m ≥ 2 (Symm² Ind_{G_{F′K}}^{G_{F′}} ψ is the sum of Ind ψ² and a character), and also for m = 1 when K ⊂ F′, so no cuspidal π of GL_{m+1} matches it (strong multiplicity one). The paper proves Theorem 1.0.1 only for E without CM: Corollary 7.1.12 needs a strongly irreducible system, Corollary 7.1.14 assumes E non-CM, and when K ⊂ F the system H¹(E) is reducible, so Corollary 7.1.13 does not apply at all. The CM case of Theorem 1.0.1 is true only in the classical isobaric sense (Deuring, Hecke), with the CM form of the Sato–Tate distribution, and the paper does not prove it. The item's own note says the Sato–Tate half 'needs E non-CM', contradicting its statement. The paper's claim that Theorem 1.0.1 (stated for every E) is 'a special case of Corollaries 7.1.13 and 7.1.14' is a gap that sourceIssues does not record. Also: Item 1's statement asserts 'Consequently the Sato–Tate conjecture holds for E' for every elliptic curve E over F. The paper proves it (Corollary 7.1.14) only for non-CM E. For E with CM, Frobenius traces are not equidistributed with respect to (2/π)√(1−t²)dt. The note says the Sato–Tate half needs E non-CM, but the statement does not. The note's parenthesis '(Corollary 7.1.14; The analytic input ...' is also unbalanced. The printed Theorem 1.0.1 omits the non-CM hypothesis, and this is not recorded in sourceIssues.

findings.claim: Item 113 folds into its statement the paper's remark 'If r̄ and r̄′ have the same associated projective representation, one is (decomposed) generic if and only if the other is.' For 'generic' (Definition 4.3.1(1)) this is false: genericity requires r̄ to be unramified, and a twist by a ramified character keeps the projective representation but is ramified. Only the decomposed-generic half is true, and its proof needs Lemma 4.3.2. No sourceIssue records this, and item 113 is planned at AG2.7 and IG.7, so a formaliser would be asked to prove the false half.
findings.evidence: The paper (published, p. 972), Definition 4.3.1(1): 'We say that a continuous representation r̄ : G_L → GL_n(k) is generic if it is unramified and the eigenvalues (with multiplicity) α_1, …, α_n ∈ k̄ of r̄(Frob_L) satisfy α_i/α_j ≠ |O_L/m_L| for all i ≠ j.' Directly after the definition: 'Note that if r̄ and r̄′ give rise to the same projective representation, then one is (decomposed) generic if and only if the other is.' (Same sentence in the TeX source.) Counterexample: p and l odd, n = 1, L = Q_l, r̄ the trivial character (unramified, and generic since there is no pair i ≠ j) and r̄′ the ramified quadratic character of G_{Q_l} with values ±1 ∈ k^×. Both have the trivial projective representation; r̄′ is ramified, so not generic. Twisting any generic r̄ of dimension n ≥ 2 by the same character gives a counterexample in every dimension. For the decomposed-generic half: if r̄′ ≅ r̄ ⊗ χ and r̄ is decomposed generic, Lemma 4.3.2 (pp. 972–973) gives infinitely many decomposed generic primes for r̄; at one above which χ is unramified, r̄′ is unramified with the same eigenvalue ratios, hence generic.

findings.claim: Item 173 (Proposition 5.4.13) omits a hypothesis that its proof needs. The proof is 'Theorems 4.3.3, 5.4.3 and Lemma 5.4.8', and Theorem 4.3.3 (Caraiani–Scholze) assumes a condition on S. For every finite place v ∉ S of residue characteristic l, either S contains no l-adic place of F and l is unramified in F, or l splits in an imaginary quadratic subfield of F. Proposition 5.4.13 does not restate this condition. The §4 analogue, Proposition 4.3.4, does restate it, as its condition (2), and Proposition 5.4.18 and Theorem 5.5.1 restate it too. In §5 it survives only as an assumption of the §5.1 set-up (item 134). As extracted, item 173 cannot be proved from Theorem 4.3.3 (item 115), whose statement carries this condition. Every use of the proposition, in the proof of Proposition 5.4.18, satisfies it.

findings.claim: The proof of Lemma 7.1.8(1) asserts 'G ≠ G^0 ≠ (0), as otherwise we would have Hodge–Tate numbers {1, 1} or {0, 0}', and then 'H ≠ H^0 ≠ (0)'. With G^0 the connected component, G = G^0 does not force Hodge–Tate numbers {1,1}. A connected l-divisible group of height 2 and dimension 1, such as that of an elliptic curve with good supersingular reduction, has Hodge–Tate numbers {0,1}. If H ≠ H^0 ≠ (0) held, H would have an étale quotient and a connected subgroup, so r̄ would be reducible and the second alternative ω_{l,2}^{−1} ⊕ ω_{l,2}^{−l} could not occur. So the proof contradicts the conclusion it states. The right condition is that G is neither étale nor of multiplicative type (dim G = 1), and that H is neither étale nor multiplicative; the supersingular case G = G^0 gives the ω_{l,2} type. The lemma stands, but the step is wrong. sourceIssues does not record this, and item 305's note copies the false step ('with G ≠ G^0 ≠ 0').

(a) Proof of Lemma 2.1.11: the integration identity is said to hold for f supported in 'U P(F)'. The right-hand side only integrates over P(F)U, and functions in ℋ(Δ, U) are supported in Δ = U_NΔ_MU_N̄ ⊂ P(F)U but not in general in UP(F). Example: GL_2(ℚ_p) with the Iwahori U, B upper-triangular, m = diag(p, 1) ∈ Δ_M and g = m·(1 0; p 1) = (p 0; p 1) ∈ Δ; writing g = ub with u ∈ U, b ∈ B(ℚ_p) is impossible.

findings.claim: The report says 'Caraiani–Scholze's generic vanishing puts the localized cohomology of the unitary Shimura variety in the middle degree (Theorem 4.3.3).' That is false for the ideals used here. The vanishing is one-sided: H^i(X̃_K̃, V_λ̃/ϖ)_m̃ = 0 for i < d and H^i_c = 0 for i > d. For m̃ = S^*(m) with m non-Eisenstein, ρ̄_m̃ is reducible, and the boundary cohomology is non-zero in many degrees. H^i(X̃_K̃)_m̃ surjects onto H^i(∂X̃_K̃)_m̃ for every i ≥ d, so it is in general non-zero above d as well. Theorem 4.3.3 gives only torsion-freeness of H^d and surjectivity onto H^d of the boundary.

findings.claim: The proof of Lemma 5.4.15 does not show that its K′ = ker(O_F^× → (O_F/𝔞)^×)·K(𝔞𝔟) is a good subgroup. In this paper a good subgroup must be a product ∏_v K_v. At the places v | 𝔟, the component of K′ is the diagonal image of the global units U = ker(O_F^× → (O_F/𝔞)^×) times ∏_{v|𝔟} K(𝔞𝔟)_v. This is a product of local groups only when the image of U in ∏_{v|𝔟}(O_{F_v}/𝔟)^× is the product of its projections, and the proof's condition on 𝔟 does not ensure that. Example: [F^+ : Q] = 2, so U = ⟨ε⟩, and 𝔟 = 𝔮_1𝔮_2 with n dividing the order of ε modulo 𝔮_1 and modulo 𝔮_2; such primes exist by Chebotarev. This 𝔟 satisfies the proof's condition ker(O_F^× → (O_F/𝔞𝔟)^×) ⊂ U^n. Then (ε, ε) lies in the 𝔟-component of K′ but (ε, 1) does not, so K′ is not a product. The conclusion det(Γ_{g,K′}) = det(F^× ∩ K′) is correct, and the lemma is plausibly true with a better choice, but the stated construction does not prove it.
